title: Who gets hired into a new firm can reflect who founded it
source_unit: CES-26-45 study using Census LEHD data and a complementary Crunchbase-LinkedIn/Revelio Labs startup sample to compare founder and worker backgrounds
geography: United States; primary LEHD analysis covers 30 states and the District of Columbia, with industry, metropolitan-area, and founding-cohort comparisons

observations.period: New-firm cohorts observed 1992-2014 in the balanced LEHD sample; paper published July 2026

denominator.unit: rounded new-firm observations in the primary balanced LEHD sample

founder_worker_similarity.value: After industry-by-metro-area-by-cohort controls, female-founded firms had a 36.4 percentage-point higher female employee share; corresponding differences were 51.2 points for Black workers, 37.3 points for Hispanic workers, and 11.3 points for non-college workers

persistence.value: Founder-background differences remained visible across firm age and persisted to at least 20 years in the unbalanced LEHD analysis

relative_wage_effect.value: Group-specific firm wage decompositions show relative wage effects for workers sharing founder characteristics ranging from approximately 2.9% to 12.9% across demographic dimensions

sample_structure.value: The balanced LEHD sample contains about 825,000 firms and 4.947 million firm-by-year observations; the complementary balanced Crunchbase-LinkedIn sample contains about 44,545 firms and 267,270 firm-by-year observations

observations.method: The primary analysis identifies new firms in Census LEHD business and wage records, uses the top three earners in a firm's first year as a founder proxy, measures employee demographic shares over firm age, and compares firms with detailed industry, metropolitan-area, and founding-cohort controls. An AKM-style wage decomposition is used to examine firm labor-demand versus worker-supply explanations. A separate LinkedIn/Crunchbase sample supplies founder-role and job-role information but has different coverage and selection.
observations.uncertainty: The LEHD data cover 30 states and D.C., not the entire country, and the balanced sample requires non-founder employees in years 0-5, MSA and industry information, and sufficient disclosure-safe observations, which selects larger or surviving firms. Founder identity is proxied by top earners in the LEHD data. LinkedIn users self-select, LinkedIn demographic measures are name-constructed, and the startup sample is skewed toward college-educated and venture-backed firms. The wage decomposition and calibrated model are not direct observations of discrimination or worker wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Female, Black, Hispanic, Asian, age, and college-education founder/worker groups, with heterogeneity by industry, metro, founding cohort, firm growth, occupation, seniority, and wage group; the primary data and complementary LinkedIn data have different units and coverage.
observations.counterinterpretation: Founder-worker similarity could reflect founder labor demand, worker supply, networks, geographic sorting, skills, firm production needs, or unobserved selection; the paper's wage decomposition favors a demand explanation but does not identify one social mechanism for every group. Similar hiring does not prove a good workplace, higher productivity, worker preference, discrimination, or durable employee security.

boundary: This record adds a founder-background-to-firm-hiring and wage-opportunity pathway. It does not establish a national employer rate, individual discrimination, worker preference, causal entrepreneurship access effects, firm culture quality, or downstream household, political, or wellbeing outcomes.
